    Chapter 7

    Message Authentication Codes: Tamper-Proof Seals

    🤔 Mallory can change a message AND recompute its hash. So how does your server know a webhook really came from GitHub?

    • ⏱️ ~4 min
    • 📚 8 sections
    • 🎮 2 interactive
    • ⭐ 200 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    7.1Why a plain hash isn't enough#

    Suppose Alice sends Bob a message plus its SHA-256 hash, so Bob can check nothing changed. Mallory intercepts it, changes the message and recomputes the hash. Bob checks: the hash matches. Fooled.

    A hash proves integrity only if the hash itself can't be replaced. To fix that, we need a secret.

    ✔ section read

    7.2MACs: a hash with a secret key#

    A MAC (Message Authentication Code) is like a hash that also uses a secret key shared by Alice and Bob:

    Analogy: a wax seal made with a signet ring. Only Alice and Bob own copies of the ring. Mallory can change the letter, but she can't make a matching seal.

    A MAC proves two things at once:

    • Integrity: the message wasn't changed.
    • Authenticity: it came from someone who knows the key.
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✔ section read

    7.3HMAC: the most popular MAC#

    HMAC turns any hash function into a MAC. HMAC-SHA256 is by far the most common.

    🧮 Math corner: HMAC hashes twice, mixing in the key two different ways:

    ipad and opad are fixed constants, and ‖ means "joined together." The double hashing defeats the length-extension attack from Chapter 6. You don't need to remember the formula; just remember to use HMAC, never hash(key + message).

    Other MACs you'll meet:

    MAC Built from Where it's used
    HMAC-SHA256 SHA-256 APIs, webhooks, JWTs, TLS 1.2, key derivation
    Poly1305 Fast math with a one-time key Paired with ChaCha20 (ChaCha20-Poly1305)
    GMAC / GHASH Galois field math Inside AES-GCM
    CMAC AES Banking and smart-card systems
    KMAC SHA-3 Newer standards
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    MAC algorithms

    ✅ Use it
    HMAC-SHA256

    Hash twice with the key

    • Works with any hash; immune to length extension
    • Supported everywhere
    • Slower than Poly1305/GMAC
    • Needs constant-time tag checks
    Best for: APIs, webhooks, JWT HS256, TOTP, HKDF
    ✅ Use it
    Poly1305

    Fast one-time MAC

    • Very fast, provable security
    • Key must be used once only (ChaCha20 handles this)
    Best for: Inside ChaCha20-Poly1305
    👍 Situational
    GMAC / GHASH

    Galois field MAC

    • Hardware fast (PCLMUL)
    • Nonce reuse breaks it badly
    • Rarely used standalone
    Best for: Inside AES-GCM
    👍 Situational
    CMAC

    MAC built from AES

    • Only needs an AES engine
    • Standardized (NIST SP 800-38B)
    • Slower than HMAC in software
    Best for: Smart cards, banking hardware
    👍 Situational
    KMAC

    MAC built from SHA-3

    • Simple: SHA-3 needs no HMAC wrapper
    • Variable output length
    • Less library support
    Best for: Newer standards
    ✔ section read

    7.4Combining encryption with a MAC#

    If you're using AEAD (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305), the MAC is already built in. But it's worth knowing how people combined them in the past, because getting the order wrong caused real attacks:

    Approach What it does Verdict
    Encrypt-then-MAC Encrypt, then MAC the ciphertext ✅ Correct: reject tampered data before even decrypting
    MAC-then-Encrypt MAC the plaintext, then encrypt both ⚠️ Caused padding-oracle attacks in old TLS (Lucky Thirteen, POODLE)
    Encrypt-and-MAC Encrypt, and separately MAC the plaintext ⚠️ The MAC can leak information about the plaintext
    AEAD All in one, designed by experts ✅ Best: use this
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Combining encryption and a MAC

    ✅ Use it
    Encrypt-then-MAC

    MAC the ciphertext

    • Rejects tampering before decrypting
    • Provably secure composition
    • Two keys and two passes to manage
    Best for: When you can’t use an AEAD
    ❌ Avoid
    MAC-then-Encrypt

    MAC the plaintext, encrypt both

    • Hides the tag
    • Must decrypt before verifying
    • Caused Lucky Thirteen and POODLE
    Best for: Old TLS (don’t copy it)
    ❌ Avoid
    Encrypt-and-MAC

    Separate MAC of the plaintext

    • Parallel
    • The MAC can leak plaintext info
    • Decrypt-before-verify
    Best for: Old SSH (don’t copy it)
    ✅ Use it
    AEAD

    All-in-one, designed by experts

    • One key, one call, one tag
    • Hard to get wrong
    • Still requires unique nonces
    Best for: Always, when available
    ✔ section read

    7.5Comparing tags safely: timing attacks#

    When checking a tag, a normal comparison stops at the first different byte. That means a wrong tag that differs at byte 1 is rejected slightly faster than one that differs at byte 20.

    An attacker can measure those tiny time differences over many attempts to guess the correct tag one byte at a time, turning an impossible 2²⁵⁶ search into a few thousand tries.

    The fix is a constant-time comparison, which always checks every byte:

    Python
    import hmac
hmac.compare_digest(received_tag, expected_tag)   # ✅ constant time
received_tag == expected_tag                      # ❌ leaks timing
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✔ section read

    7.6Where MACs are used in real life#

    • Webhooks: when GitHub or Stripe calls your server, it includes a header containing an HMAC-SHA256 of the request body made with a secret you share. Your server recomputes it to make sure the request is genuine.
    • API request signing: Amazon Web Services' "Signature Version 4" signs every API request with HMAC.
    • Session cookies: web frameworks sign cookies so users can't edit them (for example, to change user=bob to user=admin).
    • JWTs with HS256: a JSON Web Token signed with HMAC-SHA256 (Chapter 16).
    • One-time login codes (TOTP): the 6-digit codes in authenticator apps are HMACs of the current time (Chapter 16).
    • Every TLS, SSH and VPN packet: protected by a MAC or AEAD tag.
    ✔ section read

    7.7MAC vs. digital signature#

    A MAC has one limitation: both sides hold the same key. If Bob receives a tagged message, he knows it came from Alice (since he didn't send it himself). But he can't prove that to a judge: Bob could have created the tag himself.

    For public proof of who sent something (non-repudiation), you need a digital signature, which uses a private key only the sender has (Chapter 11).

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    MAC vs. signature

    ✅ Use it
    MAC

    One shared secret

    • Very fast and tiny
    • Simple key handling between two parties
    • Both sides can make tags: no non-repudiation
    • Key must be shared securely first
    Best for: Two parties who already share a key
    ✅ Use it
    Digital signature

    Private signs, public verifies

    • Anyone can verify
    • Non-repudiation
    • Slower; bigger output
    • Needs a way to trust the public key (PKI)
    Best for: Software, documents, certificates
    ✔ section read

    7.8Hands-on with HMAC#

    🧪 Try it yourself:

    Terminal
    printf 'hello' | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "secret"
# SHA2-256(stdin)= 88aab3ede8d3adf94d26ab90d3bafd4a2083070c3bcce9c014ee04a443847c0b
    Python
    import hmac, hashlib

secret_key = b"shared-secret-between-alice-and-bob"
message = b"Transfer $100 to Bob"

# Alice computes the tag and sends message + tag
tag = hmac.new(secret_key, message, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

# Bob recomputes and compares in constant time
expected = hmac.new(secret_key, message, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
print(hmac.compare_digest(tag, expected))           # True

# Mallory changes the message but can't compute a valid tag without the key
fake = hmac.new(secret_key, b"Transfer $9999 to Mallory", hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
print(hmac.compare_digest(tag, fake))               # False
    ✔ section read
